blocks.x: Okay, Buddy Burton's my name. I have recorded so on and so on. Now, cut. I'm very proud to tell you that my name is Buddy Burton, and that's my professional name when I first started recording records. And so I've been using that away from that clean up until now. What is your full name? And my full name is Evans, my first name. But after I got into the recording game and come as a fool with music, well, my recording manager made the suggestion at our first recording. He said, that name is a little bit too long. I said, Evans, you got a nickname you can use? I said, sure, I got a nickname that I'm proud of. He said, what is it? I said, Buddy. He said, well, that's a very thing. And that was Ink Williams.
Oh, yes. Mayor Williams. Mayor Williams.
I know him. And then I was under him for about ten years, I guess, contract for recording. That was when I was with the Paramount people recording with Jimmy Blythe, Jimmy O'Brien.
Oh, yes. I know him.

Great clarinet player. And then Jasper Taylor had produced the washboard on records at that particular time. And so Jasper's, and he went away on a big job. And Jimmy O'Brien, Jimmy Blythe was such close friends of mine, and he asked me if I would use this washboard in Jasper's place, because he knowed I was playing washboard as a novelty instrument all the time before Jasper started it. But I hadn't become popular like that.
Yeah.

So then I'd taken it up with Jimmy O'Brien and Jimmy Blythe. And so after we kept on with the Paramount people doing this, the novelty stuff, and so then I'd come in some fooling around, going around Jell-O'-Roll Morton, and I know each other well. So I'd come in and fooling around in with that kazoo part.
Oh, yeah.

Then I made me a little invention I'd come up with. I bought a secondhand clarinet, tore it apart, and made it shaped like a bass clarinet. And I come in some playing this thing, so Jell-O'-Roll Morton fell for it. Yeah. He liked it simply because the fellow that was playing what you call a cone, just a plain cone.
Yeah, a piece of paper on it.

And I forget his name now at that time. And anyhow, he says to me, he says, well, gee whiz, you sound almost like that cone yet, and still you got a little more power behind it. And he says, I'm going to get you to make a couple of records with me. And Jell-O'-Roll got me to make a couple of records with him and the guy on the cone and me on his own horn. And so I kept it going for a novelty use for a number of years, and so back and forth with Jimmy O'Brien, Jimmy Blythe. And so I kept on recording around that way until after years passed in between with Mayo, which we always called him Ink Williams. And so I used to try to get Ink to let me do a number by myself on piano and sing. But he always didn't have enough wax.
He was running short of wax, this, that, and the other.

So I kept on fooling around, doing those novelty numbers with washboard, playing the horn, singing and jiving, that kind of stuff until years passed in between. And Lester Melrose come along. We know him too, because he used to deal with Jell-O'-Morton during the time when I was fooling around with Jell-O, way back in the early 20s. So me and Mr. Melrose got together and got to talking. And so I said, Mr. Melrose, I said, I've got a lot of good stuff I know that could sell. He said, well what is it buddy? I said, well I want to record by myself to sing and play the piano. I said, all this is, I had a lot of recording with bands and all of their numbers. I said, but I want to do a number by myself on the piano and sing. And he said, well, what is it? You know how short they're all in the waxes? You come up with the same thing Dean Quilliams come up with now. I said, but I tell you what I do. I says, I got a couple of blues. I got some little ballad numbers and some of them semi-classic with nice words to it. And he said, well, okay then, I'll listen to them. And he come out south side there at 45th Michigan, at Jimmy Blight's house, listen to me playing and singing these things. And so at that time Papa Charlie Jackson was going big with the, he's playing the guitar and singing Uncle Bud and all them type of blues. And so Melrose had a lot of confidence in me with the different variety of numbers I was composing. He says, but he says, can't you get something together, something like Papa Charlie Jackson, and his blues is going so big? And I said, well, yeah. I said, I think I can come up with something like that. So we had a kind of a holiday after Christmas holidays was over. And we musicians got together and had a little celebration. And so they know I liked eggnog and never did too much drinking. So I got to drinking a couple of glasses of eggnog and singing and clown with the rest of them. And I come up with those blues. I call them Ham Fatsher blues. Do you remember what it was?
Yeah, I've heard.

And so after the house went down with them, so I said, well, I'll take business with pleasure. I think I'll call Mr. Melrose up tomorrow and tell him I've got just what he wants. Yeah. And that's what I did. I called him up the next day and told him, I said, Mr. Melrose, I think I've got the thing that you want, something like Papa Charlie Jackson's putting out. He said, yeah, what is it? So and so. I said, well, he said, if you show that you've got it, I'll set for the recording tomorrow morning, a special recording. He said, and you meet me at Lion Healings building. And I met him at Lion Healings building. That's when he set me up for this recording and I recorded for the Jeanette people. But the big mistake was that Melrose was, he was trying to make all the money and put out the situation. And so he called me up the very next day and had me recorded for the Paramount people.
The same number. Oh, yeah. I noticed some of those numbers there are the same thing. That's what that's what they're saying.

And that's the reason why they killed it on the market. And they had signed up for six parts to the thing. And they had them all rolled out and everything ready for it. Yeah. And I said, Mr. Melrose, you know what you're doing now. I said, won't this get us in trouble? I'll take care of all that. I said, okay. I said, I want to make money. It's true. I want to make all the money I can. So I went on down. And so, Hink Williams was standing back at the door when Jimmy Blythe was there with me. And that was the first time that Hink heard me play and sing by myself. And he thought about those ten years that he let go by then. Yeah. And he asked Jimmy, he says, whose number that is but his recording? He said, it's his own number. Why'd he get such stuff? He never let me have it. Yeah. And so then I was glad to hear him say that. So after recording, I told him, I said, that's some of the stuff I tried to get you to let me record years ago. Yeah. I says, you never had enough wax. See? I says, now Mr. Melrose sees where we can make some money out of this stuff. And we recorded, we was. We were recording every time it turned around. We were recording different numbers. So that was around my first experience of recording. And so all during this time, all recording, we'd have Johnny Dot breaking with his clarinet because Jimmy O'Brien then was the great lead for playing on the records with that washbowl band. And so every time we'd shoot Johnny Dot on it because he had a drawing card name too at that time. Yeah.
So I wonder if you could start a little bit at the very beginning, just when you were born and where too.
That was 1888, Louisville, Kentucky. Louisville.
Yeah. Do you remember that you did anybody else in your family play? Your father, mother, any brothers or anyone play? Yeah.

My mother's where the music came from because she played organ. And also she played, they were what they called a mouth organ. At that time they called it French organ. And she learned me as a kid to play the French organ. I used to play that mouth organ very good. My father and I. And so from that on up, I come in to learn on the organ. From the organ.
The regular organ like the little reed organ.
The one that you pump with your feet. Yeah. One of those that little old house organ. That you pump with your feet.
Did you have any lessons that much or take it up for yourself? No.

Only what I had taken in school. And I was self-taught. Quickly. Because my dad didn't like the idea of it. And he didn't approve of it. And so kids that those days and times with people that was, Christian people, they didn't like nothing. nothing what they called jazz or playing anything. They played some sacred, it was all right. And so that's why I used to have a lot of fun playing the sacred music and turn it into swing, which we called jazz back then, didn't they?
Did you know Glover Compton down in...
Glover Compton, I was just seeing him last week.
I saw him Saturday night, too.
I keep in touch with him. Yeah, I know Glover in Louisville, too.
In Louisville, yeah.
When he first began, when he used to be a chant and billiard player, when he didn't study about piano.
He wasn't even in music.

He was playing piano, but he wasn't interested. He was interested in the billiard. And he was always one of my favorite piano players of that type and style that he used at that time. And the same time that Glover was playing those type of houses which they had then in Louisville, you know, well, Glover was playing at one of the houses, another fellow named Jerry was playing at another, and I was playing at a small one during that time. Because Joe Glover is not much older than I.
No, I guess that... He's... You're about 71 now.
I'm 71. Mm-hmm. And so Glover, he went to Paris and stayed over there a long while and came back.
He told us all about it. We interviewed him. We interviewed him. And his wife, too. And his wife, Nettie. Yeah, singer, of course.
Yeah, they stayed together. They made quite a feel of that entertainment. She was a great entertainer, and he was, too. And so I'm sorry to hear that he had this stroke.
Yes, he's got him all right. He's doing pretty good.

He had the willpower. He was in Charlotte than anybody ever seen to have a stroke and go in and come out. So as I said, Johnny Dot, Baby Dot, and Louis Armstrong, the King Oliver, and the fellow who played trombone with them, I can't think of his name. Lil Armstrong was on piano then when they first came here.
Was it Dutre?
Dutre, or did you? And Dutre.
Dutre, the trombone player.
And Bill on the bass.
Bill Johnson, I guess.
Bill Johnson was on the bass. And Johnny Dot, he was on drums. And that was about all of the combination then.
I was going to ask you, well, I think I would sort of interrupt, but about Roy Palmer. We stopped and said hello to him yesterday. I interviewed him a couple years ago.
Yeah, yeah. I hadn't seen him for a number of years.
Did you ever make records with Roy? Do you remember? Roy Palmer is a trombone player. Yes, trombone.
Is he still living?
Yes, he just had to move. He was over on Wells Street, and they're putting in a new road down there at 51st and Wells. Yeah. And so he moved down to 68th and Perry.
68 and Perry.
16. 68 and 16 is the number.

You put that down from me, baby, because I want to get in touch with him. I'll check the number to make sure that's right. Well, I haven't seen him in so many years, and I often wondered if he was still living so many, the old time has passed away. And what an experience we had in recording.
6816 Perry. The apartment is C. There's several entrances. It's one of the big court buildings, you know, where there's several entrances. So it's the C entrance, 6816. He just moved there Wednesday.
Well, let's see.
Tore his house down Wednesday. I think he moved.
Oh, let's see, yeah.
What's his name?

Roy Palmer. P-A-L-M-E-R. The reason why this sticks out about talking about Roy Palmer, an awful experience, a sad experience, but a great experience. We went to New York to make a bunch of records under Melrose Management Center.
We had two cars. Well, Roy told me about it. You went with him once over there.

Well, and I did the driving because when we get to Philadelphia and come out of Philadelphia going to New York, we run into one of them electric snow storms. And up in the Alligator Mountains, there was no good road then. And Melrose was nervous because this recording engagement was set at this particular morning at that certain time, at that date, and he had four days engaged. And if you don't make it on time, we lose the whole four days. And so I strained myself by taking the wheel, and I says, I've had so much driving experience, I drove mostly all my life, fortunately. And so, and still driving. I said, listen, I'll tell you what we'll do. I said, we can't stop on this road. If we stop, I says, the way this snowstorm is, somebody's allowed to run into us and push us off the mountain. And I says, I'll drive at 10 miles an hour, and somebody keep wiping the windshield as much as they can. And by the time of daybreak, we'll be so near in New York, see, then we can pick up speed and get in there and make this recording engagement. Now here's where the sad part for me to come. Going through all that strain, making all that driving, all that night at 10 miles an hour, and then when daybreak come, and it did kind of let up a little bit, and then speed it up as much as it could to get into New York City. When I get into New York City, don't have time to do nothing but just take a bath and freshen up, well, that strain told on my throat. Couldn't sing. And I get down there, and I've got an, I don't know how many numbers at that time, set the record by myself that was going to help me on this recording engagement outside the Mother Normandy recording that was going to do with the band, and we had two or three different outfits with us. And that's when I started killing myself.
I was thinking you were going to say you had a wreck, but it could have been worse if you had a wreck on there.

I get up there, and here was it. One of the men dropped out on us, and Melrose says, oh, Burton says, he used to always use me to sort of this side kick, you know, along those lines, your trouble come up, and I says, well, I know a fellow here in Harlem that is a good saxophone player and a clarinet player that used to play with Ma Rainey, and he's here. And I says, I'm sure, and he made so many records with Ma Rainey, I says, he'll fit right into the picture because he knows how to handle himself and the tones and the record. And this very boy, his name was Alec Washington,
and lives right across the street here. Oh, he's here in town now. Yeah, yeah, I seen him yesterday from a distance. Elliot?

Elliot Washington. Elliot Washington. And so I says, yeah, I says, now I'll give you a number, you go down and see about him and get him and tell him I'm here and that we want him to go out and I say to so-and-so, and he'll listen to you and he'll come with you. Now, I'll take the two men down to the recording studio, which Big Bill is playing guitar and singing some blues.
Is that the Big Bill and that Brunsey that we all know?
Great, big, brown-skinned guy from, I think he was from New Orleans
or from down south or some sort. The fellow just died last year. Did he? Yes. From Mississippi. Great, big guy. Looked like he should've been
working on a railroad. Yeah, but the same
Big Bill that we know.

And Big Bill and some other guy was with us who was going to record, and he said, well, you take them down there and start their recording, and you do your single, and by that time, I'll have this guy and go to the rehearsal, get one little rehearsal in with him, and I'll bring all the rest of the men down, and we'll have it sold up for the four days. Big Bill played, the other guy played, and he comes to me to play my time. I sit down at the piano and hit the piano, and I couldn't talk about the whistle.
Oh, I was so mad
and disgusted because I was depending on this here recording, my own stuff to pay off for me. So then I had to set that all aside,
and I went on ahead
and made all the novelty instruments, numbles that they was making.
Do you remember anybody else on that trip that went over with you in the car that drove over from Chicago? By name,
I don't, there was a trumpet player named Bell. He was a New Orleans boy, too.
He was?

Yeah. His last name was Bell. Bell? Bell, and he played a very nice trumpet. And he had the New Orleans jazz, but he was as strong like Louie and the King like that. And he was originated from New Orleans. and I don't know what happened to him or to come of him since those days. Now, anybody else outside Rona Parma and Big Bill and this Al Washington, he's up in his 60s, you know, Al, since he was a young man than I was. And I said, I know him from a kid. That's about all I can remember during that
dad recording. That's a big deal because most people don't remember who, Roy didn't remember who those fellows were except you. He mentioned you.
He remembered me, you see, and I remember Bill, Roy, and Big Bill. And I can't remember, there was quite a few of them that bunch, but I just can't remember the names.
Oh, I was going to ask, you mentioned once you were down in New Orleans a few months or a couple of months and played there, did you?
Yeah,
I,

the last, the last time that I played there, I played with Butter Beans and Susie Shaw. Oh, yeah. Old man, Eddie Haywood, had the band and I was playing drums and all. See, I doubled on drums too. Oh,
you did on drums.

Yeah, and I was playing drums in the orchestra with Eddie Haywood and we had trumpet and sax. We'd always carry along and then we'd, in the towns like New Orleans, another place where we'd rather increase our band than we'd add those extra men to it. We kept the four regular with us like that. And so, we played two different theaters in New Orleans that I can't remember the name and then we played a returning game and we played four different times and the closest I can remember that last time was around 1930s, the early 30s. I dare say, around about in the 31st, when I was down there that last time.
When you first went there, did the music seem much different? Did they have a different beat or a different style than you'd been playing? The same way that I would love
to tell, if I could express myself as exactly like I feel about this music that they continue to talk about on air that they call, or, what do they call this that the kids does now? Well, Bach.
Oh yeah,

rock and roll. Rock and roll. The whole thing, is the same stuff that I played and we played years ago before World War 1 from New Orleans to Louisville and Louisville and all up and down there and Memphis, Tennessee, we played that same stuff, but they called it jazz then. And then they had, they had a bunch of youngsters that came out at that time, was dancing during my younger brother's days and I got it from him, the slang that they used to use and they called it rug cutting. Oh yeah. And one of the numbers that I recorded for the Paramount people that I picked up on and put some words to it and called it the barefoot stomp.
Remember that.

That was one of my numbers that I used as a novelty number because they used to use those two terms. If they didn't say that we was going out rug cutting, we was going to a barefoot stomp. and the all was done with the same motion and the same identical movement from the different types of youngsters. They would, most of them that would, what do I call, clown real big that they have a couple of mixed drinks in them and they'd clown a little more than the others.
And as I said, I played for some of that stuff and I listened
to them on radio and TV explaining about this year and they've given a different name and different generations.
It's the same old music.
It's the same old music that we have warmed over and over. It's the old original jazz and now it's the modern swing.
I wonder if you could tell a little bit about the first time you met Jolly Roll Martin. You say you remember him when you first came to Chicago.

First time, first time that I met him in person. I know him and seen him time and time again. I had a red hot five piece band at 31st and State and at that time I was called the Kentucky Midnight Serenaders and I was the first one that originated that day and the boys in the band was, they was all tops, that was all. Louis Armstrong and old man King Oliver didn't have nothing on my trumpet player and they used to come down there Louis, King Oliver and his whole band would come and watch us.
What we did
for this five, this trumpet player that I had then with me was Ray, Ray, Ray, Ray, Ray. It's Raymond and Ray. We called him Shorty Mack.
Shorty Mack. I'll find his name somebody else. We called him Shorty Mack. He was born
in Evanston and he had a kind of hunchola and it was short and he could play the sweetest trumpet with a mute in it in an apartment where we would go to some of them
bedtime house, you know,

and me always was knowing that we were very soft on piano and I'd play on soft piano and you could just hardly hear him play and he could play every jazz technique that Joe and Louis and he was Louis.

to ask you if you knew

heard that name.

And she was one of Clarence Jones the scholars and she was a genius at the piano. And she could cover tense with just laying her hands on the piano with full harmony. I brought her from the west side over here to the south side and I organized this little band and the reason I mentioned her about her being a genius in which nobody on the south side knows she was a great classic and I schooled her in how to swing and jazz and I know that she could take classics and cut them up and improvise it in this jazz form. And my ideas of playing jazz all the time because I played around them white saloons in Louisville and I had to play the national hammering and everything in jazz temple to get my money. And so I was used to that. And so when I got this little band and brought them out there I used all that kind of stuff because the type of band that I had was men in a band that could play that stuff and improvise it. Now to help me to get this stuff arranged like that my cousin was a great artist in music and you might know of him Dr. Charlie Cook.
Oh yes. I met him years ago.

Well now when he had his ranging office down in Lyon Healy building I went down there and explained to him what I was in for and what I wanted to do. I said Margie Lewis is a great pianist. I said you have never seen her. I said but I know that she can cut it. I said she can hold so much harmony on the piano and I got a trombone player from Louisville that used to play violin and could play trumpet and he could take trombone and play off a violin sheet and play the leads and he could sing tenor and so we're all doubling like that and the trumpet player could double on violin which was Ray Mack I said I want you to arrange me a nice little arrangement and a melody in F in the jazz form see and he said what do you want to take a number like that buddy and cut it up like I said will you arrange this with a small arrangement and fill it full harmony so that I can produce this thing out there I said something new he said well I laughed like if you want it that way I'm going to fix that way and I'm coming out and listen to see what it sounds like that is the first beginning of that type of a musician taking classics and arranging them into swing form Charlie Cook could you

My name is Bob Schaffler. They called me Bob Schaffler. My name is Robert L. Schaffler, Robert Lee Schaffler. What the musician called me, Bob Schaffler. Where were you born? Just when? I was born in Bessie, Tennessee, April the 30th, 1900.
So just about 59 years old now.
That's right. And my people brought me to St. Louis when I was two years old of course. I knew more about St. Louis than I knew about Bessie, Tennessee.
Did any of your folks play music? Your father or another?
No one in my family played music.
Any brothers or sisters that were interested in? I have no brothers or sisters. Do you remember the first music you heard? What kind of music you heard in St. Louis?

Well the first music I heard was what they had a Cudded band called the Nice Epiphance Cadet Band. And I started playing in that band as a drummer. That was back in 1906. Did you have any lessons on the drums? Did you just pick it up? No. See, at that time they called them the Nice Epiphance Cadets. It's the same at the present time as you'd have the Boy Scouts. Oh yes, yes. You know, but just the kids in the neighborhood. They used to all. And this nice Epiphance was an organization that took all the kids off the street so they had some place to go. And they had a man by the name of Colonel Hughes we called him. And he took us and learned us how to drill, regular formation drill. And they organized the band. The first he joined us the trumpet and bugle horn. And of course I was playing drums then. We had a leader by the name of Blue, Professor Blue, who was the trumpet player. But he had lost his lip. His lip had split straight down and he couldn't play no more. But he was interested in children. So he said he was a trainer. For some reason or another he liked me and he put me off the drums and gave me a bugle.
Oh yes.
But he was leading up to the trumpet.
